models.family: a piecewise trend times a weekly season times a holiday effect
models.purpose: Forecast the number of Wordle reports and explain the swings.
models.summary: The trend is a piecewise line whose slope jumps at the changepoints, and the jump size follows a Laplace distribution scaled by tau. The weekly term is a Fourier sum, and the holiday term adds one coefficient for each named holiday. The forecast multiplies the trend, the season, the holiday, and a residual. The fit uses pyStan on the log of the counts, with 60 changepoints, tau of 0.8, and a changepoint range of 0.9. Five holidays are named. The transpose mark in the trend is printed as a capital gamma.

models.family: three player groups with infection, fatigue, and return
models.purpose: Explain the rise and the fall of the report count.
models.summary: Twitter users are split into ordinary users, players, and tired players, mapped onto the susceptible, the infected, and the recovered. Ordinary users become players with probability lambda, players tire with probability beta, and tired players return with probability eta. All three groups can leave at a rate theta. The player count is said to come from solving the differential equations and is then scaled to the report count. No equation is printed. The fitted curve is said to conform to the Prophet trend.

models.family: a least-squares line from word attributes to the hard-mode share
models.purpose: Test whether the word attributes change the hard-mode share.
models.summary: The hard-mode share is the hard-mode reports over all reports. The line puts an intercept and one slope on each attribute, plus an error. The attributes are the frequency, the letter-frequency sum, the number of different letters, the breadth of usage, the letter counts, and the part of speech. The fitted line is sent to the appendix because of its length. The F statistic is 1.058 and the p-value is 0.379, so the line is not significant. The null sets every coefficient, including the intercept, to zero.

models.family: a one-hidden-layer network on borrowed word vectors
models.purpose: Predict the share of players who solve the word in each number of tries.
models.summary: The word attributes from the first task are normalized and reduced, then joined to pre-trained GloVe vectors. The network has one hidden layer of 1024 units, a ReLU activation, and a dropout of half the units. The loss is an L2 norm, the optimizer is Adam, the learning rate is 0.05, and the weights start from a Xavier draw. Negative outputs are set to zero and the rest are rescaled so they sum to one. The training is repeated and the best run is kept, because the draw and the dropout change the result.

models.family: a three-group clustering of words by their try shares
models.purpose: Sort the words into easy, medium, and hard.
models.summary: The seven try shares are the inputs. The distance is Euclidean, and the number of groups is set to three by the elbow chart together with the authors' experience of game difficulty. The groups hold 135, 156, and 68 words and are labeled easy, medium, and hard from the share of players who need five or more tries, which is 25.35, 39.92, and 58.59 percent. A later principal-component plot is used to argue the groups separate, and the method is ranked above two alternatives by a silhouette coefficient and a Calinski-Harabasz score.

models.family: a binomial test on the first letter of the hardest words
models.purpose: Find which first letters make a word hard.
models.summary: The difficulty of a word is the share of players who need five or more tries. The hardest fifth of the words is kept. Under the null, a letter starts such a word with probability 0.2, and the count of hard words for that letter is binomial. A letter is called out when its tail probability falls below 0.05. The letters e, f, and w are called hard, and e is called the hardest. The letter t is called the easiest by the same test run on the other tail.
